title: CRLF reaches a flat key=value session file on a branch that skipped the encoder, and a cache/promote path turns the injected lines into real records
index_line: T-0019 · AUTH_DECISION · separator injection into a key=value store, hidden by a second representation until promoted · perl/php/ruby/python · corroborated
invariant_violated: A flat `key=value` session file is treated as a structured store, so a value is assumed to stay a value. That holds only if every write path escapes the separator — and the write path that matters is the one that skips the encoder because an optional field is absent. A separate serialised cache then hides the injection from the reader that matters, until a maintenance path re-serialises the raw file and promotes the injected lines to top-level keys.

mechanism.does: the attacker obtains a session *name* by failing a login — the server mints a pre-auth session and writes it to disk
the presented credential travels in an HTTP auth header and is written back into the session record
the encoder that would encode the field is conditional on an optional component of the session cookie
newline/separator bytes inside the value are written verbatim, so the following bytes land as additional top-level records with attacker-chosen key names
the primary reader prefers a serialised cache in which the whole payload sits inside one value — the injection is invisible there
a pre-auth reachable maintenance path reads the raw file (cache disabled), re-serialises it, and writes both representations
the loader now answers 'is this session an administrator' from attacker-chosen records, and the session is trusted

source.http.header.value: the Authorization: Basic credential (base64) — the value whose field is written back into the store; this is why the injection is pre-auth

sink.file.write.value: the session file itself: a flat key=value (or key|serialized) store whose records are line- or separator-delimited

encoding.string.value: CRLF / separator bytes carried inside the value field, plus a first byte of junk so the legitimate key still parses

guard.escaping.value: the per-field sanitiser and the conditional encoder — the guard exists, is applied to some fields and some write paths, and skips this one

sync.window.value: two representations must disagree, then be reconciled by a maintenance path; the attacker needs the promote step to happen before the check

preconditions.expr: sessions are persisted in a flat delimiter-separated file per session (not a signed opaque cookie, not a database row)
a value the attacker supplies is written back into the session record on an error path (failed login, denial, retry counter)
the sanitiser is per-field and a write path exists that does not call it (check the callers, not the definition)
the target exposes a pre-auth reachable path that reads the raw store with the cache disabled and re-serialises it (that path is what promotes the injection)

success: the on-disk session file shows the injected pairs as siblings of the legitimate keys (`cat -A` shows the line breaks)
the serialised cache initially does NOT show them at top level — the two representations disagreeing is the signature
after the promote path runs, the cache and the loader both report the attacker-chosen key, and the authorisation decision flips
failure_like: the value is encoded (hex/base64) on every write path — the separator never reaches the file
the store's parser rejects unknown keys, or the loader re-validates the record set against a schema
the session name is not attacker-obtainable, or the optional cookie component cannot be omitted without a 400
false_positive: a session file that contains newlines because it was hand-edited or corrupted — the test is whether an *attacker-supplied* value produced them
authorisation that appears to flip because of a client-side flag, a stale cookie, or admin UI caching
a 30x redirect after the injection proves the credential was accepted, not that the injected records were read

hazards: there are two representations and they disagree on purpose — auditing only the file, or only the cache, gives the wrong answer in both directions
the guard is not missing, it is applied to the wrong set: audit the *callers* of the sanitiser, and the branches that skip optional encoding
path resolution that strips the optional cookie component means omitting the component does not change which file is addressed
non_transfers: opaque, signed session tokens (JWT, Rails encrypted cookies) — there is no server-side record to inject into
stores that serialise as JSON/msgpack with a real encoder on every path
a loader that reads one representation only — then the injection either works immediately or never, and the 'hidden then promoted' step does not exist
